summary: Defines the NOTIFY message in DNS, which lets a primary server tell its secondary servers right away that a zone has changed. The secondaries can then ask for the update instead of waiting for a timer to expire.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a DNS server that keeps a copy of someone else's zone waits for a timer before checking whether anything changed. NOTIFY is a message that says changed, so the copy can be refreshed at once.

questions: how do dns slaves learn about zone changes
what is a stealth dns server
does dns notify use udp or tcp
subtitle: Lets a DNS master tell its secondaries that a zone has changed.

tldr.problem: Secondaries usually learn that a zone changed by waiting for a refresh timer to expire, so a change can take a long time to reach every copy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a NOTIFY opcode, sent as an ordinary DNS message, in which a master tells its secondaries that the zone has changed so that they can start a query immediately instead of waiting.
tldr.outcome: The master still keeps its load low, because a second copy of the zone is still fetched by transfer, but the delay between a change and the secondaries catching up is much shorter.

today: RFC 1996 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Notify Instead of Poll
sections.content:
Slow propagation of new and changed data in a DNS zone can be due to a zone's relatively long refresh times. Longer refresh times are beneficial because they reduce the load on the master servers, but that benefit comes at the cost of long intervals of incoherence among authoritative servers whenever the zone is updated.

The DNS NOTIFY transaction allows master servers to inform slave servers when the zone has changed, an interrupt as opposed to a poll model, which is hoped to reduce propagation delay while not unduly increasing the masters' load. This specification only allows slaves to be notified of SOA record changes, but the architecture of NOTIFY is intended to be extensible to other record types.

The document also gives more definition to the roles of master, slave and stealth servers, their enumeration in NS records, and the SOA MNAME field. In that sense it can be considered an addendum to RFC 1035.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting on a timer keeps the server quiet but makes the data stale for longer. NOTIFY lets the master say changed right away, and the secondaries then do the work of fetching the new copy.

sections.title: The Server Roles
sections.content:
The document defines the roles precisely. A slave is an authoritative server that uses zone transfer to retrieve the zone, and all slave servers are named in the NS records for the zone. A master is any authoritative server configured to be the source of zone transfer for one or more slaves. The primary master is the master server at the root of the zone transfer dependency graph, is named in the zone's SOA MNAME field and optionally by an NS record, and by definition there is only one per zone. A stealth server is like a slave except that it is not listed in an NS record; unless explicitly configured otherwise it sets the AA bit in responses and is capable of acting as a master, and other servers will only know of it if given static configuration data indicating its existence.

The Notify Set is the set of servers to be notified of changes to a zone. The default is all the servers named in the NS record set, except any server also named in the SOA MNAME. Some implementations let the administrator override this set or add elements to it, for example stealth servers.

The zone's servers must be organised into a dependency graph with a primary master, and all other servers must use AXFR or IXFR either from the primary master or from some slave that is also a master. No loops are permitted in the AXFR dependency graph.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one head server for a zone, and a set of servers that copy from it. NOTIFY goes to the ones in that set.

sections.title: The NOTIFY Message
sections.content:
When a master has updated one or more records that slave servers may be interested in, it may send the changed record's name, class, type and optionally new data to each known slave using a best-efforts protocol based on the NOTIFY opcode.

NOTIFY uses the DNS message format, although it uses only a subset of the available fields. Fields not otherwise described are to be filled with binary zero, and implementations must ignore all messages for which this is not the case.

NOTIFY is similar to a query in that it has a request message with the QR flag clear and a response message with QR set. The response contains no useful information, but its reception by the master indicates that the slave received the NOTIFY, so the master can remove the slave from any retry queue for that event.

The transport is UDP unless the master has reason to believe TCP is necessary, for example if a firewall between master and slave allows only TCP, or if the changed record is too large to fit in a UDP datagram. If TCP is used, both sides must continue to offer name service during the transaction even when it is not making progress. The NOTIFY request is sent once, and a timeout is said to have occurred if no response arrives within a reasonable interval.

If UDP is used, a master periodically sends a NOTIFY request to a slave until too many copies have been sent, an ICMP message indicates that the port is unreachable, or a NOTIFY response arrives with a matching query ID, QNAME, source IP address and source UDP port number. The interval between transmissions and the total number of retransmissions should be operational parameters that the administrator can set, perhaps per zone. Reasonable defaults are a 60 second interval, or a timeout if using TCP, and a maximum of 5 retransmissions for UDP, with additive or exponential backoff considered reasonable for the retry interval.

A NOTIFY request has QDCOUNT greater than zero and the other counts at least zero. If ANCOUNT is greater than zero, the answer section is an insecure hint at the new record set for that name, class and type, and a slave that receives such a hint is free to treat equivalence with its local data as a sign that no further work is needed. If ANCOUNT is zero, or the answer differs from the slave's local data, the slave should query its known masters to retrieve the new data. In no case may the answer section be used to update a slave's local data, to indicate that a zone transfer needs to be undertaken, or to change the slave's zone refresh timers. This version of the specification makes no use of the authority or additional data sections, so conforming implementations should set those counts to zero when transmitting requests, and current implementations must ignore those sections if they are present, but not the entire message.
sections.plainLanguage: It is an ordinary DNS message with a new operation number, sent over UDP and repeated a few times until the other side answers. The answer the other side sends back carries no data; it only says the message arrived.

sections.title: What a Slave Does on Receipt
sections.content:
The only defined NOTIFY event at this time is that the SOA record has changed. When the transaction for QTYPE=SOA completes, the slave should behave as though the zone had reached its REFRESH interval: it should query its masters for the SOA of the zone named in the NOTIFY, and check the answer to see whether the SOA serial has been incremented since the zone was last fetched. If so, a zone transfer, either AXFR or IXFR, should be initiated.

Because a deep dependency graph may have several paths from the primary master to a given slave, a slave may receive a NOTIFY from one of its known masters even though the others have not yet updated their copies. The query for the zone's SOA should therefore be directed at the known master that was the source of the NOTIFY, and not at the other known masters. This is a departure from RFC 1035, which specifies that when the SOA REFRESH interval expires, all known masters should be queried in turn.

If a slave receives a NOTIFY request from a host that is not a known master for the zone containing the name in the question, it should ignore the request and record an error in its operations log. This implies that slaves of a multihomed master must either know their master by the closest of the master's interface addresses, or know all of the master's interface addresses, or a valid request might come from an address that is not on the slave's list of masters for the zone, which would be an error.
sections.plainLanguage: On receiving the message the second copy checks the zone's serial number with the server that sent it, and if the number has gone up it fetches the new zone.

sections.title: Details and Examples
sections.content:
Retaining query state across host reboots is optional, but it is reasonable to execute an SOA NOTIFY transaction on each authority zone when a server first starts.

Each slave is likely to receive several copies of the same NOTIFY request: one from the primary master, and one from each other slave as that slave transfers the new zone and notifies its potential peers. The protocol supports this multiplicity by requiring that NOTIFY be sent by a slave or master only after it has updated the SOA record or has determined that no update is necessary, which in practice means after a successful zone transfer. Thus, barring delivery reordering, the last NOTIFY any slave receives is the one indicating the latest change.

If a master wants to avoid causing a large number of simultaneous outbound zone transfers, it may delay for an arbitrary length of time before sending a NOTIFY to any given slave. The time is expected to be chosen at random, so that each slave begins its transfer at a unique time, and the delay shall not in any case be longer than the SOA REFRESH time. The RFC suggests random delays of between 30 and 60 seconds would be adequate if the servers share a LAN and the zones are of moderate size.

A slave that receives a valid NOTIFY should defer action on any subsequent NOTIFY with the same name, class and type until it has completed the transaction begun by the first one, since this duplicate rejection avoids having multiple notifications lead to pummelling the master server.

The message details are given as field lists. When the zone has updated on the primary master, it sends a NOTIFY request to all servers named in the Notify Set, with a new query ID, op NOTIFY (4), resp NOERROR, the AA flag, qcount 1, the zone name as qname, the zone class as qclass and T_SOA as qtype. When a slave that is also a master updates the zone, the same applies, except that its Notify Set may differ because of optional static specification of local stealth servers. When a slave receives a NOTIFY request from one of its designated masters with QTYPE=SOA and QR clear, it enters the state it would if the refresh timer had expired, and sends a NOTIFY response back to the source with the same query ID and with QR also set. When the master receives that response, it deletes the query from its retry queue, completing the notification process for that change and that server.
sections.plainLanguage: Copies of the message arrive from several servers, and the last one wins because a server only sends after it has the new data. The master can also stagger when it tells each server, so that they do not all fetch at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document believes the NOTIFY operation has only two security considerations.

First, a NOTIFY request with a forged IP and UDP source address can cause a slave to send spurious SOA queries to its masters, leading to a benign denial of service attack if the forged requests are sent very often.

Second, TCP spoofing could be used against a slave server given NOTIFY as a means of synchronizing an SOA query, and UDP or DNS spoofing as a means of forcing a zone transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the message carries no proof of who sent it, someone could send fake ones to make the secondaries do extra work. The effect is a slowdown rather than anything worse.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF A NOTIFY REQUEST

items.label: QTYPE
items.desc: The only defined NOTIFY event is a change to the SOA record.

items.label: Flags in the request
items.desc: The authoritative answer bit is set in the request.

items.label: Flags in the response
items.desc: Clear in a request, set in the response.

items.label: QDCOUNT
items.desc: A NOTIFY request carries one question entry.

items.label: Default retry interval
items.desc: Also the timeout when TCP is used.

items.title: Forged source address
items.text: A slave can be made to send pointless SOA queries to its masters, a benign denial of service if sent often.

items.title: Spoofed transfers
items.text: TCP spoofing could synchronise an SOA query and UDP spoofing could force a zone transfer.
